# How many congressional districts are there in the United States?

March 22, 2026· Updated November 7, 2026 by [What District Am I In?]

There are **435 congressional districts** in the United States, each represented by 1 member of the U.S. House of Representatives. This number has remained fixed since 1913, when Congress passed legislation capping the House at 435 seats. The Permanent [Apportionment] Act of 1929 made this cap permanent.

## Congressional districts by state

The 435 districts are divided among the 50 states by population. California has the most with 52, followed by Texas with 38 and Florida with 28. 6 states have a single [at-large district]: Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

## Which state has the most congressional districts?

California has the most congressional districts, with 52. Texas is next with 38, then Florida with 28 and New York with 26. Illinois and Pennsylvania have 17 each. The fewest is 1 at-large district, in 6 states: Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

## How districts are divided among states

Every state is guaranteed at least 1 congressional district, but beyond that, seats are allocated based on population. After each census, a mathematical process called apportionment determines how many of the 435 seats each state receives. Currently, the states with the most districts are California (52), Texas (38), Florida (28), and New York (26). 6 states have just one [at-large] district: Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, and Wyoming.

## How big is each district?

Based on the 2020 Census total population of approximately 331 million people, each congressional district contains roughly 760,000 residents. However, this varies somewhat because districts must be drawn within state boundaries, Montana’s 2 districts each have about 542,000 people, while Delaware’s single district covers nearly 990,000.

## Should there be more districts?

Some reformers argue that 435 seats are too few for a country of over 330 million people. When the cap was set in 1913, each district represented about 212,000 people, less than a third of today’s average. Proposals to expand the House range from modest increases to plans like the Wyoming Rule, which would set district size based on the smallest state’s population, potentially creating over 500 seats.

Want to explore every one of the 435 districts? [Browse our complete directory] or [find your district by ZIP code].

## From 65 seats to 435

The House did not always have 435 members. The first Congress in 1789 had 65 representatives. As the country added states and people, the House grew after almost every census, reaching 435 by 1913. Congress then fixed the size with the Reapportionment Act of 1929, which set a permanent ceiling and a formula for dividing the seats. The number has stayed at 435 ever since, even as the U.S. population more than tripled, so each district now represents far more people than it did a century ago.

## Districts, seats and the 6 non-voting members

The 435 districts are the voting seats in the House. 6 other places each send a non-voting member: the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands. These delegates, and the resident commissioner from Puerto Rico, can serve on committees and vote in committee, but they do not have a vote on the House floor, so they are not part of the 435.

## States with a single district

6 states are small enough in population to have just 1 at-large district that covers the entire state: Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, and Wyoming. Their lone representative serves the whole state rather than one slice of it. Every other state is divided into 2 or more districts, up to 52 in California, the most of any state.

## When the number changes

The national total stays at 435, but the share each state receives can change every 10 years. After each census, the seats are reapportioned among the states using a method called equal proportions. Faster-growing states gain seats and slower-growing states lose them. After the 2020 census, for example, Texas gained 2 seats and several states each lost one, while the total stayed exactly 435.

## Why 435?

Nothing in the Constitution requires 435 seats. The Constitution says only that each state gets at least 1 representative and that seats are apportioned by population, with no district smaller than 30,000 people. Congress capped the number at 435 in the early twentieth century to keep the chamber from growing unwieldy, and changing it would take a new act of Congress. That is why the figure has held steady for more than a hundred years.

The **2020 United States census** was the 24th decennial [United States census]. Census Day, the reference day used for the [census], was April 1, 2020. Other than a pilot study during the [2000 census],[[1]] this was the first U.S. census to offer options to respond online or by phone, in addition to the paper response form used for previous censuses.[[2]]

The census was taken during the [COVID-19 pandemic], which affected its administration. The census recorded a resident population of 331,449,281 in the 50 states and the national capital of [Washington, D.C.], reflecting an increase of 7.4%, or 22,703,743, over the [2010 census].[[3]] The growth rate was the second-lowest ever recorded, and the net increase was the sixth-highest in history. This was the first census where the ten most-populous states each surpassed ten million residents, and the first census where the ten most-populous cities each surpassed one million residents.

This census's data determined the electoral votes' distribution for the [2024 United States presidential election]. A subsequent review by the [Census Bureau] found significant miscounts in several minority populations and in several states.

## Background

[[edit]]

[![Image 7]]

A 2020 U.S. census yard sign in [Columbus, Ohio]

As required by the [United States Constitution], the U.S. census has been conducted every 10 years since 1790. The 2010 United States census was the previous census completed. All people in the U.S. 18 and older are legally obligated to answer census questions, and to do so truthfully ([Title 13 of the United States Code]).[[4]][[5]][Personally identifiable information] is private and the Census Bureau itself will never release it. However, the [National Archives and Records Administration] could release the original census returns in 2092, if the [72-year rule] is not changed before then.[[6]]

On census reference day, April 1, 2020, the resident United States population (50 states and Washington, D.C., excluding overseas territories and military members and civilian U.S. citizens living abroad) was projected to be 329.59 million,[[7]] a 6.76% increase from the [2010 census].

## Purpose

[[edit]]

### Reapportionment

[[edit]]

See also: [United States congressional apportionment]

[![Image 8]]

Allocation of [U.S. congressional] districts following the 2020 census

The results of the 2020 census determine the number of seats for each state in the [House of Representatives], hence also the number of electors for each state in the [Electoral College], for elections from 2022 to 2032.

The Census Bureau announced the apportionment figures on April 26, 2021. 13 states had changes in congressional seats:

* [California], [Illinois], [Michigan], [New York] "New York (state)"), [Ohio], [Pennsylvania], and [West Virginia] lost one seat.[[8]]
* [Colorado], [Florida], [Montana], [North Carolina], and [Oregon] gained one seat.
* [Texas] gained two seats.

This represented a smaller number of seats shifting than was forecast by independent analysts.[[9]]

### Redistricting

[[edit]]

See also: [2020 United States redistricting cycle]

State and local officials use censuses to redraw boundaries for districts such as congressional districts ([redistricting]), state legislative districts, and school districts.

### Federal funding distribution

[[edit]]

Dozens of federal programs use census data to help direct funding to state and local areas. Census results help determine how more than $675 billion in federal funding are allocated to states and communities each year for roads, schools, hospitals (health clinics), emergency services, and more.[[10]]

## Major design changes

[[edit]]

The 2020 census was the first U.S. census to offer a full internet response option and the first to extensively use technology instead of paper to manage and conduct fieldwork.[[11]]

Key design changes included:[[2]][[12]]

* Three response options: Internet, paper, and phone. Ultimately, every household that did not respond online was sent a paper form. Households in areas with low internet access received a paper form from the start.
* Multiple languages: In addition to English, respondents were able to complete the census in 12 other languages on
